```{python}
#| label: setup
import os, warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
# MVBBSC (the live B-MV row) draws 4 NUTS chains via NumPyro; give JAX four host
# devices so they run in parallel on a single-CPU renderer (set before any JAX import).
os.environ.setdefault("JAX_PLATFORM_NAME", "cpu")
os.environ.setdefault("XLA_FLAGS", "--xla_force_host_platform_device_count=4")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import Markdown

def _find_up(name, start, hops=6):
    d = os.path.abspath(start)
    for _ in range(hops):
        if os.path.exists(os.path.join(d, name)):
            return d
        d = os.path.dirname(d)
    return os.path.abspath(start)

ROOT = _find_up("basedata", os.getcwd())
BASE = os.path.join(ROOT, "basedata")
DATA = os.getcwd() if os.path.exists(os.path.join(os.getcwd(), "data", "basc_weights.csv")) \
    else os.path.join(ROOT, "review", "basc_westgermany")
DATA = os.path.join(DATA, "data")
```

## The question

The authors write in their responses "*we have removed the normalization step and re-run the entire West Germany analysis using the original per-capita GDP scale, consistent with the standard setup of Abadie et al. (2010, 2015). Accordingly, the description of the normalization procedure has been removed from Section 5, and all empirical results have been updated, including the posterior donor inclusion probabilities, donor weights, counterfactual trajectories, credible intervals, and the estimated treatment effects. The revised results lead to the same substantive conclusions as those reported in the previous version.*" By this, I take them to mean "we took the original West Germany data (that was un-transformed) and ran SCM, BASC, and the others through this exact dataset." It is against this claim that I view the second round of review.

On the BASC side that claim checks out, and I want to say so plainly before raising anything else. The authors' public sampler (`BASC_realdata.R` at `github.com/sll-lee/paper-BASC`) prepares the outcome as `y <- raw.y` and the donor matrix as `x <- t(raw.x)`, commented "Final manuscript version: original per-capita GDP scale". The pre-1990 mean and standard deviation are still computed there but no longer applied. Running that sampler myself, on much shorter chains than the paper's, returns a post-1990 ATT in the range -390 to -702 against the paper's reported -434, and selects the same three donors the paper's own Table 7 does. So BASC itself is on the scale the authors say, and it reproduces.

The difficulty is with the four methods BASC is compared against, none of which appear in that repository at all.


BASC is presented as a competitive-or-superior synthetic-control estimator. Because the credibility of any synthetic control rests, to some degree, on how well it reproduces the treated unit's pre-intervention outcome trajectory, a minimum bar for such a claim is the pre-treatment fit for the new method compared to those of the standard tools in the SCM literature. Below I compare BASC's in-sample (pre-1990) fit on West Germany against `mlsynth`'s own estimators on the identical data (the Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller 2015 `repgermany` panel, original per-capita GDP scale), assembled with `mlsynth`'s `compare_estimators` utility. The `mlsynth` analyses run at render time; BASC is precomputed (its Gibbs sampler runs from the authors' R, `github.com/sll-lee/paper-BASC`).

## Specifications

Standard SCM (s-SCM, per the paper) is run from `mlsynth` in two ways. The first is outcome-only, matching the pre-1990 GDP path. The second uses covariates, in the canonical Abadie et al. (2015) predictor set:

- GDP per capita, inflation rate, trade openness, industry share — averaged **1981–1990**;
- investment rate and schooling — averaged **1980–1985**.

We estimate the fit via two bilevel solvers: `backend="malo"` and `backend="mscmt"` (MSCMT's nested differential-evolution search). The robust family is `CLUSTERSC` (RPCA-SC and PCR/RSC). As a benchmark outside the SCM family entirely, we also include `FDID`, the forward-selected difference-in-differences estimator of Li (2024).

```{python}
#| label: compare
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from mlsynth import VanillaSC, CLUSTERSC, FDID, MVBBSC, compare_estimators

# --- ADH 2015 West Germany covariate specification ---
COVS = ["gdp_avg", "infrate", "trade", "industry", "schooling", "invest80"]
WINDOWS = {"gdp_avg": (1981, 1990), "infrate": (1981, 1990), "trade": (1981, 1990),
           "industry": (1981, 1990), "schooling": (1980, 1985), "invest80": (1980, 1985)}
FIT_WINDOW = (1960, 1989)          # outcome-matching (pre-treatment) window

raw = pd.read_stata(os.path.join(BASE, "repgermany.dta"))
d = raw[["country", "year", "gdp", "infrate", "trade", "industry", "schooling", "invest80"]].copy()
d["gdp_avg"] = d["gdp"]             # GDP per capita as an averaged predictor
d["treat"] = ((d.country == "West Germany") & (d.year >= 1990)).astype(int)

base = dict(df=d, outcome="gdp", treat="treat", unitid="country", time="year",
            display_graphs=False)
cov = dict(covariates=COVS, covariate_windows=WINDOWS, fit_window=FIT_WINDOW, seed=0)

# One panel, several specifications -> compare_estimators does the rest
cmp = compare_estimators({
    "VanillaSC (outcome-only)":    VanillaSC({**base}),
    "VanillaSC (malo, ADH cov)":   VanillaSC({**base, "backend": "malo",  **cov}),
    "VanillaSC (mscmt, ADH cov)":  VanillaSC({**base, "backend": "mscmt", **cov}),
    "CLUSTERSC (RPCA-SC)":         CLUSTERSC({**base, "method": "rpca", "rpca_method": "PCP"}),
    "CLUSTERSC (PCR/RSC)":         CLUSTERSC({**base, "method": "PCR"}),
    "FDID (Forward DID)":          FDID({**base}),
    "B-MV (MVBBSC, mlsynth)":   MVBBSC({**base, "n_warmup": 500, "n_samples": 500,
                                           "n_chains": 4, "seed": 0}),
}, show_bands=False)
```


```{python}
#| label: load-basc
basc_cf = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA, "basc_counterfactual.csv"))        # 2000/2000
basc_cf500 = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA, "basc_counterfactual_500.csv")) # 500/500
basc_w = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA, "basc_weights.csv"))
bmv_cf = pd.read_csv(os.path.join(DATA, "bmv_counterfactual.csv"))          # B-MV via bsynth
```

## In-sample (pre-1990) RMSE by method

```{python}
#| label: tbl-rmse
tbl = (cmp.summary.rename(columns={"pre_rmse": "In-sample RMSE", "att": "ATT"})
       .reset_index().rename(columns={"method": "Method"}))
tbl = tbl[["Method", "In-sample RMSE", "ATT"]]

# BASC in-sample RMSE and post-1990 ATT from each saved posterior counterfactual
# (ATT = mean(observed - synthetic) over 1990+, the same convention as cmp.summary).
def _basc_rmse_att(cf):
    pre, post = cf["year"] < 1990, cf["year"] >= 1990
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((cf.loc[pre, "observed"] - cf.loc[pre, "synthetic"]) ** 2)))
    att = float((cf.loc[post, "observed"] - cf.loc[post, "synthetic"]).mean())
    return rmse, att

rmse_2000, att_2000 = _basc_rmse_att(basc_cf)
rmse_500,  att_500  = _basc_rmse_att(basc_cf500)
# 25000/25000: reported from a single long offline chain (seed 200). Its posterior
# counterfactual is not stored or plotted; the exact script and the commit that
# produced these two numbers are in the reproducibility appendix at the end.
rmse_25k, att_25k = 195.516, -389.799
basc_rows = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Method": "BASC (25000 / 25000 MCMC)", "In-sample RMSE": rmse_25k,  "ATT": att_25k},
    {"Method": "BASC (2000 / 2000 MCMC)",   "In-sample RMSE": rmse_2000, "ATT": att_2000},
    {"Method": "BASC (500 / 500 MCMC)",     "In-sample RMSE": rmse_500,  "ATT": att_500},
])
rmse_bmv, att_bmv = _basc_rmse_att(bmv_cf)
bmv_row = pd.DataFrame([
    {"Method": "B-MV (bsynth, Bayesian SCM)", "In-sample RMSE": rmse_bmv, "ATT": att_bmv},
])
full = pd.concat([tbl, bmv_row, basc_rows], ignore_index=True).sort_values("In-sample RMSE").reset_index(drop=True)
Markdown(full.round(1).to_markdown(index=False))
```

Every comparison estimator attains a materially tighter pre-treatment fit than BASC. BASC's pre-1990 RMSE sits in a ~170–195 band across the three chain lengths (burn-in/sampling: 500/500, 2000/2000, 25000/25000), roughly 3 times the plain `VanillaSC` fit (60.8), and about twice the `CLUSTERSC` (88.6 / 98.0) and `FDID` (83.4) fits. Lengthening the MCMC does not close the gap; if anything the best-mixed 25000/25000 chain fits worst.

The most telling row is B-MV, the Bayesian synthetic control of Martinez and Vives-i-Bastida (2024). This is the model BASC is built on, before the donor-selection layer is added. Run the original `bsynth` package in its standard outcome-only mode (`predictor_match = FALSE`) on this same panel and B-MV fits the pre-1990 path at RMSE 62.2; `mlsynth`'s `MVBBSC` returns 62.1. Both tie `VanillaSC` (60.8). Adding the donor-selection layer, on this dataset, costs about three times the pre-treatment fit of the model it is added to, and that comparison is internal to the paper's own lineage — it does not depend on any estimator I have chosen.

A note on what in-sample fit can and cannot show. BASC performs selection, so some in-sample loss is expected by construction, and a Bayesian posterior mean is shrunk in a way that a least-squares optimum is not. Neither consideration accounts for the gap here, because B-MV carries the same Bayesian machinery, the same Gaussian-process term and the same posterior-mean summary, and fits at 62.

## The reported effects do not sit together


The paper's five ATT estimates (p.32) are -434 for BASC, -218 for B-MV, -159 for standard SCM, -1,655 for fPCA-SYNTH and -2,427 for ClusterSC, all described as per-capita units. Set them beside what the same methods return on the same panel:

| Method (paper's label) | Paper's ATT (p.32) | Reproduced here | Reproduced pre-1990 RMSE |
|---|---|---|---|
| BASC | -434 | -390 to -702 (authors' own sampler) | 169-195 |
| ClusterSC | -2,427 | -1,501 / -2,039 (`CLUSTERSC` RPCA / PCR) | 88.6 / 98.0 |
| fPCA-SYNTH | -1,655 | not reproduced here | -- |
| B-MV | **-218** | **-2,075 (`bsynth`) / -2,079 (`MVBBSC`)** | 62.2 / 62.1 |
| standard SCM | **-159** | **-1,298 (`VanillaSC`)** | 60.8 |

The first three rows are unremarkable: BASC reproduces, and the paper's ClusterSC and fPCA-SYNTH figures are the same order of magnitude as what the corresponding estimators return. Whatever scale the paper is on, it is one on which an effect of -1,655 or -2,427 is reportable.

A caveat on the BASC row, in the authors' favour. My chains are far shorter than theirs: 500/500, 2,000/2,000 and 25,000/25,000 against the paper's three chains of 500,000 after 500,000 burn-in, which Section 5 reports as converged with Gelman-Rubin below 1.01 and diagnoses further in Appendix C.2. Across my three the ATT moves over -702, -583 and -390 without settling, so I do not read the gap from the reported -434 as a discrepancy — it is most likely my burn-in, and the reported value has the better claim to being the converged one.

What matters for this report is that the in-sample fit is not similarly unstable. It stays in a 169 to 195 band across a fiftyfold change in chain length, and the shortest and longest chains bracket the same conclusion. The fit finding does not depend on chain length; the ATT reproduction does, and I am not resting anything on it.

That is what makes the last two rows hard to explain. B-MV and standard SCM are reported an order of magnitude smaller than they come out, and these are the only two of the four comparison methods I can check independently — standard SCM because the paper prints its weight vector in Table 7, and B-MV because two implementations of it exist. A single mis-scaled outcome would have moved all five numbers together; it has not. Whatever produced -218 and -159 was applied to those two methods and not to the other three.

The direction is also one-sided. At -159 and -218, BASC's -434 sits unremarkably among its comparators, larger than the two classical benchmarks and smaller than the two robust ones. At the values those methods actually return, -1,298 and -2,079, BASC is the smallest estimate in the table by a factor of three, and the ordering that supports the paper's competitiveness claim on this application does not survive. I make no claim about how this arose. I do think it has to be resolved before the West Germany application can be read as evidence for the method.

On B-MV specifically: `mlsynth`'s `MVBBSC` is a NumPyro re-implementation of the Martinez and Vives-i-Bastida model written from the paper, not from `bsynth`'s code, so the agreement between them (-2,079 against -2,075, credible bands agreeing year by year) is a genuine cross-check and not a translation. Reconciling the reported B-MV with what the method returns is for the authors to do.

I want to be clear about how much weight this section carries, because it is the part of my report the authors are most likely to answer, and answering it would not settle the review. Suppose every reported ATT is confirmed as computed on the raw per-capita series exactly as stated, and the -218 and -159 turn out to be correct for whatever was actually run. The two findings that motivate this report are untouched. BASC's pre-1990 fit is still three times worse than the model it extends, and the weight vector printed in Table 7 still fits the pre-1990 path worse than uniform weights do. Neither of those is an inference from the ATTs; both are computed from the pre-treatment period alone, on the original scale, and one of them uses nothing but the authors' own published numbers.

```{python}
#| label: fig-paths
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
cmp.plot(ax=ax)                                   # mlsynth methods + observed
ax.plot(basc_cf["year"], basc_cf["synthetic"], color="#d62728", lw=2.2,
        label="BASC", zorder=5)
ax.axvspan(basc_cf["year"].min(), 1990, color="0.92", zorder=0)
ax.axvline(1990, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_title("West Germany: observed vs synthetic counterfactuals")
ax.set_xlabel("year"); ax.set_ylabel("GDP per capita")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

BASC's own posterior path, with its 95% credible band, is below. The band is worth a second look on its own account, separately from the fit.

```{python}
#| label: basc-coverage
_pre = basc_cf[basc_cf["year"] < 1990]
_in = ((_pre["observed"] >= _pre["lo95"]) & (_pre["observed"] <= _pre["hi95"]))
Markdown(
    f"In the pre-treatment period the 95% credible band contains the observed West "
    f"German series in **{int(_in.sum())} of {len(_pre)}** years, with a mean band "
    f"width of **{float((_pre['hi95'] - _pre['lo95']).mean()):.0f}** per-capita units."
)
```

This is a calibration point, not a fit point, and it cuts against reading the wide posterior as appropriate humility. The band is narrow — its mean pre-treatment width is about the size of the pre-treatment RMSE itself — and it nonetheless excludes the series it is modelling in two thirds of the years where the truth is observed. A 95% interval that misses in-sample two-thirds of the time is not expressing uncertainty about a well-centred fit; it is a tight interval around a path that is in the wrong place. Whatever the post-1990 credible intervals in Figure 5 are doing, the pre-1990 record gives little reason to trust their nominal coverage.

```{python}
#| label: fig-basc-ci
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.axvspan(basc_cf["year"].min(), 1990, color="0.92", zorder=0)
ax.fill_between(basc_cf["year"], basc_cf["lo95"], basc_cf["hi95"], color="#d62728", alpha=0.15, label="BASC 95% CI")
ax.plot(basc_cf["year"], basc_cf["synthetic"], color="#d62728", lw=2, label="BASC synthetic")
ax.plot(basc_cf["year"], basc_cf["observed"], color="black", lw=2.4, label="West Germany (observed)")
ax.axvline(1990, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set_xlabel("year"); ax.set_ylabel("GDP per capita")
ax.set_title("BASC posterior counterfactual (2000/2000)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Which donors BASC keeps

The fit gap has a readable cause in the donor set. The canonical ADH 2015 solution for West Germany is sparse and led by Austria and the USA (published weights: Austria 0.42, USA 0.22, Japan 0.16, Switzerland 0.11, Netherlands 0.09); `VanillaSC` on this panel recovers the same two units at the top. BASC assigns both a weight of zero.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-basc-weights
w = basc_w.copy()
w["weight"] = w["weight"].round(3)
w["incl_prob"] = w["incl_prob"].round(3)

# cmp.weights is long-form: one row per (method, donor)
vsc = dict(zip(*(cmp.weights.loc[cmp.weights.method == "VanillaSC (outcome-only)",
                                 ["donor", "weight"]].to_numpy().T)))
w["VanillaSC"] = [round(float(vsc.get(n, 0.0)), 3) for n in w["donor"]]
# the paper's own Table 7 BASC column (CSDA-D-25-01439R1, p.31), posterior means
paper_basc = {"USA": 0.00, "UK": 0.00, "Austria": 0.00, "Belgium": 0.00, "Denmark": 0.00,
              "France": 0.00, "Italy": 0.12, "Netherlands": 0.00, "Norway": 0.00,
              "Switzerland": 0.44, "Japan": 0.37, "Greece": 0.01, "Portugal": 0.05,
              "Spain": 0.00, "Australia": 0.00, "New Zealand": 0.00}
w["BASC (paper Table 7)"] = [paper_basc[n] for n in w["donor"]]
w = w.rename(columns={"donor": "Donor", "weight": "BASC (reproduced)",
                      "incl_prob": "incl. prob."})
Markdown(w[["Donor", "BASC (paper Table 7)", "BASC (reproduced)", "incl. prob.", "VanillaSC"]]
         .to_markdown(index=False))
```

My reproduction and the paper's Table 7 select the same three donors — Switzerland, Japan and Italy — and agree that every other unit, Austria and the USA included, receives essentially nothing. The two columns differ on how the mass is split between them (Italy 0.30 against the paper's 0.12, inside the paper's own reported standard deviation of 0.14), which is the sort of disagreement two runs of the same sampler produce. Taken with the ATT agreement (-390 against -434), this is a reproduction of the authors' method, so what follows about its fit is a statement about BASC and not about my ability to run it.

Dropping Austria and the USA is a substantive choice, not a numerical detail. These are the two donors that carry the ADH solution, and BASC assigns them posterior inclusion probability 0.000 and 0.014. A method whose selling point is donor selection excluding the donors the canonical analysis of this dataset relies on is a result the paper should confront directly.

## The reported "standard SCM" weights (Table 7)

A separate problem sits in the paper's Table 7, which reports each method's West Germany donor weights. The "standard SCM" (s-SCM) column is essentially uniform. The weights are roughly 0.04 to 0.05 on every donor, with a single 0.34 spike on Spain. However, the genuine ADH solution is sparse and led by Austria. Those weights are the entire s-SCM model — standard SCM has no other moving part — so its in-sample fit is just their dot product with the donor GDP series, which any reader can check against the authors' own numbers.

I apply this test only to the s-SCM column, and deliberately. BASC and B-MV add a Gaussian-process term to the weighted donor average, so for those two the weights alone do not determine the counterfactual and a dot product would misrepresent the model. For standard SCM there is nothing else to add.

```{python}
#| label: tbl7
#| echo: true
#| code-fold: false
from mlsynth.utils.datautils import dataprep

# Canonical reshape: dataprep returns the treated vector, the donor matrix (aligned
# to donor_names), and the pre/post split
prep = dataprep(d, "country", "year", "gdp", "treat")
y7 = np.asarray(prep["y"]).flatten()
D7 = np.asarray(prep["donor_matrix"])
names7 = list(prep["donor_names"])
pre7 = prep["pre_periods"]

# Table 7 "standard SCM" weights (CSDA-D-25-01439R1, p.31)
s_scm = {"USA": .05, "UK": .05, "Austria": .05, "Belgium": .05, "Denmark": .05, "France": .04,
         "Italy": .04, "Netherlands": .04, "Norway": .05, "Switzerland": .04, "Japan": .04,
         "Greece": .03, "Portugal": .04, "Spain": .34, "Australia": .04, "New Zealand": .05}

def dot_fit(wdict):
    syn = D7 @ np.array([wdict[n] for n in names7])         # synthetic = donor_matrix . weights
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y7[:pre7] - syn[:pre7]) ** 2)))
    att = float(np.mean(y7[pre7:] - syn[pre7:]))
    return round(rmse, 1), round(att, 1)

rmse_s, att_s = dot_fit(s_scm)
rmse_u, att_u = dot_fit({n: 1 / 16 for n in names7})
Markdown(pd.DataFrame({
    "Weight vector": ["s-SCM (Table 7)", "uniform (1/16)", "VanillaSC"],
    "pre-1990 RMSE": [rmse_s, rmse_u, 60.8],
    "post-1990 ATT": [att_s, att_u, -1297.5],
}).to_markdown(index=False))
```

Two things follow, using only the authors' own weights. First, the s-SCM column fits the pre-1990 path at an RMSE near 1,925. This is worse than uniform weights (about 1,289), and roughly 30 times greater than the actual synthetic control (about 61, reported above). A weight vector that loses to uniform is not the standard-SCM solution, whatever produced it. Second, those same weights imply a post-1990 ATT near +2,900, with West Germany above its synthetic, while the paper's text (p.32) reports an s-SCM ATT of -159 — the opposite sign. So the reported vector is not the optimum, and the table and the text disagree with each other. Even setting `mlsynth`'s `VanillaSC` aside entirely, the Table 7 s-SCM column and the reported s-SCM effect cannot both come from the same estimator, and I would like an explanation of why.

The table prints weights to two decimals, so it is fair to ask whether that rounding is doing the damage. It is not. Perturbing the sixteen weights independently within the full printing error and renormalising to the simplex, over 4,000 draws, moves the pre-1990 RMSE only within 1,861 to 2,002 and leaves the implied ATT positive in every draw (2,731 to 3,088). The conclusion does not depend on the printed precision.

```{python}
#| label: tbl7-rounding
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
w0 = np.array([s_scm[n] for n in names7])
_r, _a = [], []
for _ in range(4000):
    wp = np.clip(w0 + rng.uniform(-0.005, 0.005, size=w0.size), 0, None)
    wp = wp / wp.sum()
    syn = D7 @ wp
    _r.append(np.sqrt(np.mean((y7[:pre7] - syn[:pre7]) ** 2)))
    _a.append(np.mean(y7[pre7:] - syn[pre7:]))
Markdown(pd.DataFrame({
    "Quantity": ["pre-1990 RMSE", "post-1990 ATT"],
    "as printed": [rmse_s, att_s],
    "min over rounding": [round(min(_r), 1), round(min(_a), 1)],
    "max over rounding": [round(max(_r), 1), round(max(_a), 1)],
}).to_markdown(index=False))
```

The picture makes it unmistakable. Drawn on the same axes, a correctly solved standard SCM (`VanillaSC`) and the Bayesian SCM the paper builds on (`MVBBSC`) are indistinguishable from observed West Germany through the pre-1990 window, while the counterfactual implied by the Table 7 s-SCM weights sits well below it the entire time.

```{python}
#| label: fig-three-scm
#| fig-cap: "West Germany: observed versus a correctly solved standard SCM (VanillaSC), the Bayesian SCM the paper builds on (mlsynth's MVBBSC), and the counterfactual implied by the paper's own Table 7 s-SCM weights. The two correctly computed fits are indistinguishable from observed West Germany across the pre-1990 window (shaded); the Table 7 weights sit below it the entire pre-period, so their implied post-1990 effect comes out positive -- the wrong sign."
def _curve(label):
    s = cmp.curves[cmp.curves["method"] == label].sort_values("period")
    return s["period"].to_numpy(dtype=float), s["counterfactual"].to_numpy(dtype=float)

yr_v, cf_vsc = _curve("VanillaSC (outcome-only)")
yr_m, cf_mvb = _curve("B-MV (MVBBSC, mlsynth)")
cf_t7 = D7 @ np.array([s_scm[n] for n in names7])          # Table 7 weights . donor matrix

wg  = d[d.country == "West Germany"].sort_values("year")
yrs = wg["year"].to_numpy(dtype=float); obs = wg["gdp"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
_pre = yrs < 1990
_rmse = lambda cf: float(np.sqrt(np.mean((obs[_pre] - cf[_pre]) ** 2)))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.axvspan(yrs.min(), 1990, color="0.92", zorder=0)
ax.axvline(1990, color="grey", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.plot(yrs,  obs,    color="black",   lw=2.6, label="West Germany (observed)", zorder=6)
ax.plot(yr_v, cf_vsc, color="#1f77b4", lw=2.0, label=f"Standard SCM (VanillaSC), pre-RMSE {_rmse(cf_vsc):.0f}", zorder=5)
ax.plot(yr_m, cf_mvb, color="#2ca02c", lw=2.0, label=f"B-MV (mlsynth MVBBSC), pre-RMSE {_rmse(cf_mvb):.0f}", zorder=5)
ax.plot(yrs,  cf_t7,  color="#d62728", lw=2.2, ls="--", label=f"Table 7 s-SCM weights, pre-RMSE {_rmse(cf_t7):.0f}", zorder=4)
ax.set_title("West Germany: observed vs. three standard-SCM counterfactuals")
ax.set_xlabel("year"); ax.set_ylabel("GDP per capita")
ax.set_xlim(yrs.min(), yrs.max())
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper left"); ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Bottom line

In my opinion, in order for us to continue reviewing this, the authors' GitHub page needs to be updated. **Not just** with their own BASC code, but with everything that went into producing these results. That is, we must be able to verify the importing of the data, the cleaning process that was done, the exact runs of fPCA-SC/ClusterSC they used, the exact code they used to produce B-MV, and the exact solver they used to produce the s-SCM weight vector in Table 7. Further, the authors must report not just the ATT, but the in-sample RMSE that each method produces, so that their claims may be directly checked against the syntax they used.

This request is narrower than it may sound, because the repository as it stands supplies exactly one of the five methods in Table 7. `github.com/sll-lee/paper-BASC` contains `BASC_realdata.R` and the `repgermany` data, and that script runs the BASC sampler and nothing else. There is no code in it for standard SCM, B-MV, fPCA-SYNTH or ClusterSC. `tidysynth` is declared in the script's package list and never called anywhere in the file, which is the only trace of a comparison method in the repository. So of the four comparison estimators, none can currently be reproduced by a reader, and the two I could check by other means are the two whose reported effects I cannot obtain.

Two smaller points on the repository, offered as housekeeping. The README's structure block names `BASC_basc_realdata.R` and its run instructions say `source("clean_basc_realdata.R")`, while the file that is actually present is `BASC_realdata.R`; neither of the documented names exists. And the README says the data file may be absent for licensing reasons, but `data/repgermany.dta` is in fact committed.

To be clear: I recognize that in-sample fit is not the sole determining factor in the validity of a novel SCM. For example, in the original Robust SC and Robust PCA SC papers by Amjad and Bayani respectively, the authors remark that their denoising solutions are desirable because they attain similar results as the original method without the need to match on predictors. As we can see here, these results hold even though PCR, clustered PCR/RPCA SC attain slightly worse in-sample fit compared to the baseline model from ADH 2015. However, it is not my belief that BASC attains comparable in-sample fit compared to the baseline toolkit. BASC does not even compete with the Forward DID method (a uniformly weighted subset of controls plus an intercept). The paper claims competitiveness to the baseline toolkit in simulation studies, but the competitiveness on the canonical datasets has not yet been demonstrated.


## Reproducibility: the offline benchmarks

The toolkit rows run at render time. The BASC 500/500 and 2000/2000 rows and the B-MV row are regenerated at render time from saved posterior counterfactuals; the BASC 25000/25000 row is a single long offline chain reported as a bare pair of numbers (in-sample RMSE 195.516, post-1990 ATT -389.799). The scripts and data behind the offline pieces are given below so each can be reproduced against a known state of this repository.

```{python}
#| label: stamp
#| echo: false
import subprocess
def _git(*a):
    try:
        return subprocess.run(["git", *a], capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=ROOT).stdout.strip() or "unknown"
    except Exception:
        return "unknown"
Markdown(f"Reproduced against `mlsynth` at commit `{_git('rev-parse', '--short', 'HEAD')}` "
         f"({_git('log', '-1', '--format=%ci')}).")
```

The chain uses the authors' own sampler (`safe_chol` ... `run_basc_chain` from
`github.com/sll-lee/paper-BASC`, sourced as `basc_funcs.R`) on the West Germany
outcome and 16-donor matrix exported from `basedata/repgermany.dta`. It is
identical to `scripts/basc_run.R` except for the chain length, and is shown here,
not executed.

```r
# BASC on West Germany, 25000 burn-in + 25000 sampling (single chain, seed 200).
#   -> in-sample (pre-1990) RMSE = 195.516,  post-1990 ATT = -389.799
suppressMessages(library(MASS))
rinvgamma <- function(n, shape, scale) 1 / rgamma(n, shape = shape, rate = scale)
rtmvnorm <- function(n, mean, sigma, upper, ...) {   # q=1, diagonal, upper-truncated
  sdv <- sqrt(diag(as.matrix(sigma))); qd <- length(mean); out <- numeric(qd)
  for (i in seq_len(qd)) {
    p <- pnorm((upper[i] - mean[i]) / sdv[i])
    out[i] <- mean[i] + sdv[i] * qnorm(runif(1, 0, max(p, 1e-12)))
  }
  matrix(out, nrow = 1)
}
rdist <- function(x1, x2 = NULL) {
  x1 <- as.matrix(x1); if (is.null(x2)) x2 <- x1 else x2 <- as.matrix(x2)
  outer(seq_len(nrow(x1)), seq_len(nrow(x2)),
        Vectorize(function(i, j) sqrt(sum((x1[i, ] - x2[j, ])^2))))
}
source("basc_funcs.R")                        # authors' safe_chol .. run_basc_chain

y  <- as.numeric(read.csv("y.csv", header = FALSE)[, 1])    # West Germany GDP (44)
x  <- as.matrix(read.csv("x.csv", header = FALSE))          # 16 donors x 44 years
vt <- seq_len(length(y)); Dt <- as.integer(vt >= 31)        # treatment from 1990
j <- ncol(x); t <- length(vt); N <- 25000; nburn <- 25000   # (paper uses 500000/500000)

chain <- run_basc_chain(seed = 200, y = y, x = x, vt = vt, Dt = Dt, N = N, nburn = nburn, q = 1)

g <- chain$gamma.sample; u <- chain$u.sample
beta <- matrix(0, N, j); for (i in 1:N) beta[i, ] <- (g[i, ] * u[i, ]) / sum(g[i, ] * u[i, ])
y.samp <- matrix(0, N, t)
for (i in 1:N) y.samp[i, ] <- as.numeric(x %*% beta[i, ] + chain$f.sample[i, ])
cf <- colMeans(y.samp); pre <- vt < 31; post <- vt >= 31
cat(sprintf("in-sample RMSE = %.3f   post-1990 ATT = %.3f\n",
            sqrt(mean((y[pre] - cf[pre])^2)), mean(y[post] - cf[post])))
```

The B-MV counterfactual (`data/bmv_counterfactual.csv`) is the Martinez and
Vives-i-Bastida (2024) Bayesian SCM computed with the authors' cited `bsynth`
package (Ignacio Martinez's implementation, `github.com/ignacio82/bsynth`), built
from source and run as

```r
bayesianSynth$new(data = repgermany, time = year, id = country, treated = D,
                  outcome = gdp, ci_width = 0.95, predictor_match = FALSE)$fit(cores = 4)
```

on the `repgermany` panel (`D = 1` for West Germany from 1990) — the same
outcome-only configuration as bsynth's own West Germany example. Its posterior-mean
counterfactual gives pre-1990 RMSE 62.2 and post-1990 ATT -2075.
